As per the case of the prosecution, on 06.11.2015, at about 06.00 p.m., the defacto complainant and his wife were proceeding in their Swift Car bearing Registration No.TN 09 AZ 4249 in front of the Kokirakulam Collector Office.

While they were proceeding on the Melapalayam Road, A1 to A3 wrongfully restrained them, opened the back door of the car, pulled out the wife of the defacto complainant and assaulted her with hands, they damaged the front glass shield of the car by stricking it with hands and threatened them saying that they would set them on fire.

After completion of investigation, the Police has filed a charge sheet against the accused.

5. After completing the legal mandates, charges have been framed against A1 and A2 for the offence under Sections 341, 323, 506 (ii) IPC, Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Women Act, 2002 and Section 3 of Tamil Nadu Public Property (Prevention of Damage and Loss) Act.

convicted and sentenced them as mentioned supra.
Aggrieved over that, the appellants have preferred this appeal.

10. The law was set in motion based on the complaint given by P.W.1 on 06.11.2015 i.e., on the very day of occurrence itself.
He stated in the complaint that on 06.11.2015, he picked up his wife in his swift car bearing Registration No. TN09AZ4249, at about 06.00 pm.
At about 06.00 pm., while he Sorimuthu @ Suresh vs State Rep on 8 August, 2025

3 was driving the car in front of Collectorate Office, Tirunelveli Corporation, the accused were walking on the road.
P.W.1 gave a honk to alert them.
However, the accused became enraged and unlawfully restrained the vehicle and questioned P.W.1 on how he dared to honk at them.
They then opened the backside door of the car and pulled his wife out and assaulted her and they also criminally intimidated her by threatening to kill her.
P.W.1 came out from the car and he was also beaten up by all the three accused.
The second accused broke the front windshield of the car by striking it with his hand.
The first accused damaged the side-view mirror on the left side of the car by kicking it.
He also stated that the accused had kicked his wife on her chest and kicked him on his stomach and beat on his cheeks.

. Since P.W.1 and the accused are utter strangers, there cannot be any previous motive for the complainant to give a false complaint against the accused.
Even the appellants have also not stated that the accused were already known to the complainant , P.W.1.
P.W.1, in his evidence, has stated all the details, which was stated by him in the complaint.
There are some minor discrepancies, but the over all evidence of P.W.1 is seen to be consistent with the complaint.
The cross-examination of P.W.1 did not bring out anything material to disbelieve his evidence given in the chief examination.
12. P.W.2, wife of P.W.1, has also given evidence corroborating the evidence of P.W.1 in all materials aspects.

She has stated that she was sitting in the rear seat and the accused were waiting to cross the road, at that time, her husband, P.W.1 gave the horn, upon which, the accused got enraged and unlawfully restrained the car and the passengers of the car and shouted at P.W.1 for giving horn and opened the backside door and pulled her out and thereafter, the first accused kicked her on her chest.
When her husband rushed out of the car, the accused 2 and 3 beat him with their hands.
The second accused had damaged the front windshield of the car by striking it with his hands.
When she screamed, the first and second accused beaten her and her husband.
Nothing is brought out during cross- examination to discredit her evidence in chief.

The injured witnesses, P.W.1 and P.W.2, on the day of occurrence, at about 10.00 pm., have been examined by P.W.4, doctor.
P.W.4 had stated in her evidence that P.W.1 did not have any visible external injury, but she had stated that some three persons have beaten him with hands.
In respect of P.W.2, the doctor has stated that P.W.2 might have been attacked by three persons and she also did not have any visible external injuries.
However, the doctor has stated that when someone beats a person with hands and legs, it is possible that no visible external injury may be present, but a person may still experience pain.
The doctor ought to have inquired about the pain suffered by the victims and recorded the same.
Unfortunately, the doctor was not specific or diligent enough to ask such question despite the significance of medicolegal cases especially at the time of registering AR.
The fact remains that P.W.1 and P.W.2 have clearly stated how they were affected by the incident.
Even though P.W.1 and P.W. 2 were advised admission, they chose not to get admitted.

15. P.W.6 stated that he received the complaint from P.W.1, registered FIR and referred P.W.1 and P.W.2 to the hospital for treatment.
The investigating officer stated that during his enquiry, P.W.1 disclosed the names of the accused.

Although P.W.1 has initially sated that three identifiable persons have assaulted him, the investigating officer appears to have specifically asked P.W.1 how he came to know the names of the accused, for which, P.W.1 has stated that he has made enquiry with his relatives and through them, he came to know about the names of the accused.
The investigating officer also ascertained the identity of the accused by conducting enquiry into the matter.

He also sent the vehicle for inspection and got the report which is marked as Ex.P.5.
16.
It is claimed by the learned counsel for the appellants that P.W.1 and 2 are interested witnesses and there is no independent witnesses in this case.

Since the occurrence had taken place in a public place, it would have been prudent for the investigating officer to have examined any witnesses, who may have been present in the place of occurrence at the the relevant point of time.

As the accused had behaved in a violent manner, everyone https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on:
08/10/2025 04:17:25 pm ) Crl.A.(MD)Nos.232 and 307 of 2017 present would have got frightened to identify the accused.

Therefore, it cannot be reasonably expected that the independent witnesses would have had the courage to provide evidence supporting the testimonies of P.W.1 and P.W.2.
17.

Only if the evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2 are found to be unreliable in view of any significant reasons, the Court is required to seek the corroborative evidence that might be available through some independent witnesses.
Since P.W.1 and P.W.2 are the injured witnesses and victims, there exists no plausible motive for them to wrongly identify the accused.
18. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the witnesses have stated after going to the hospital that they did not return to the police station.
However the investigation officer sated that P.W.1 and P.W.2 had come back to the police station after returning from the hospital and thus it was contended that there is a contradiction.
But it cannot be considered as a major contradiction that could affect the very case of the prosecution.
As it pertains only to incidental facts that arose subsequent to the occurrence, the above contradiction can be ignored as a minor contradiction.

Hence, its impact on the overall case of the prosecution is https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis (

While appreciating the evidence in a holistic manner, the minor contradictions need to be overlooked.
19. Unless the evidence of injured witnesses, P.W. 1 and P.W.2, is tainted by any motive, there is no reason to doubt their evidence.
The occurrence took place on a public road, where P.W.1, the driver of the car, was driving the car by having P.W.2 also in the car.

It is quite natural for drivers to honk Sorimuthu @ Suresh vs State Rep on 8 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125731781/

sentences.text: If the honk irritates any individual and make them impatient, it is the individual's tendency and the driver of the car cannot be blamed.
The accused 1 to 3 appeared to have been overly sensitive and had shown an unnatural irritation to an extent of quarreling with P.W.1.

Their inappropriate and disproportionate emotion did not end there, they exhibited the audacity to forcibly pull out P.W.1's wife, who was sitting on the back seat, by opening the car door and they even kicked her.
Such indecent and barbaric conduct exhibited by the accused in the public view would have no doubt caused shame, embarrassment and pain to a woman like P.W.2.
The trial Court has rightly appreciated the evidence and held the accused guilty for the commission of the offence under Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Woman Act.

The accused also attacked both P.W.1 and P.W.2 with their hands.
Although P.W.1, was alone and helpless, he was trying to protect himself and his wife for the extent possible, but the accused continued to assault him.
The act of the accused was not only violent, but also indecent to the extent of outraging the modesty of a woman.
The witnesses have clearly spoken in their evidence as to how the accused had unlawfully restrained the car from proceeding further and attacked them by blowing their hand and legs.
21. They have also described the damage caused to the vehicle including the breaking of the front windshield.

22. The learned counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the TNPPDL Act is applicable only when the damage is caused on a private property; only if the occurrence that had taken place during procession, assembly, meeting agitation and demonstration and other activities, it can come under TNPPDL Act.
This aspect has been settled by the Division Bench of this Court in the judgment held in Mangalanatha Durai and others vs., State, 2023/MHC/2505, in Crl.R.C.(MD)No.869 of 2022.

As there are conflicting view on the above point, the Division Bench has settled it by stating that when the charging provisions of the Act being clear and https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis (

The relevant paragraphs of the above judgment are extracted as under:
.......27.

We are therefore constrained to conclude that the charging provisions of the Act being clear and unambiguous, taking recourse to the statement of objects and reasons so as to give a restricted interpretation to the enactment is not justified.
We therefore overrule those judgments and approve the judgments in Venkataesam v. State; Giri v. State; Balu v. Jayaganthan; and R.Mokkamayan v. State.

3.The learned counsel for the petitioner would submit that the nature of injuries clearly made out the offence under 'Section 307 of IPC' as per the Judgement passed by the Honourable Supreme Court in the case State of M.P. v. Harjeet Singh reported in 2019 (20) SCC 524.

sentences.text: Further the accused caused damages to the properties worth about Rs.1,00,000/-.

Hence, in all fairness, the investigating agency, should have included TNPPDL Act, as per the order of the Division Bench of this Court in Crl.R.C.(MD).No.869 of 2022, which was confirmed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in S.L.P.Crl.No.11692 of 2023, observing that TNPPDL Act is applicable to the private property also.

Therefore, it cannot be claimed by the appellants that with the aid of the ruling that was overruled that the private property incidents can be considered only in the light of the statement and not by the object of the Act without giving the relevant, unambiguous and clear provisions found in the site.
25. It is further submitted that the damage has not been assessed by a person qualified to assess the damage and give an evaluation certificate in this regard.

In support of the above contention,
reference was made to the judgment of this Court held in Kumar Vs., State rep., by Inspector of Police in Crl.A.No.57 of 2019, dated 28.03.2022, in which it has been held as under:
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 08/10/2025 04:17:25 pm )
Crl.A.(MD)Nos.232 and 307 of 2017 .......17.
Now on coming to the conviction under Section 3 (1) of TNPPDL Act, it is the case of the prosecution that during the time of occurrence, accused damaged the property to the tune of Rs.1,00,000/-.
In this regard, admittedly the 'value of the damage' certificate has not been produced.

In fact, in the Motor Vehicles Inspector's Report issued by the P.W.11 under Ex.P9, he had advised the investigation officer to collect the loss certificate from the automobile engineer, but the investigation officer in this case, without complying with the advice given by the Motor Vehicles Inspector, filed a final report alleging that the appellant is guilty under Section 3 (1) of TNPPDL Act. ......

sentences.text: In the said circumstances, herein it is a case being the reason that the value of the damage has not been brought to the court, this Court is not in a position to decide whether the act committed by the accused is an ordinary mischief or offence punishable under Section 3(1) of TNPPDL Act.

Therefore in the said circumstances, we cannot hold that the accused herein is liable to be convicted under the said provisions of the TNPPDL Act......
26.
In the above case, the Motor Vehicle Inspector advised the investigating officer to collect loss certificate, but in the instant case he did not give any direction.
Now, it is not a question of assessing the damage caused to the vehicle in order to grant any compensation.
The trial Court had imposed only fine and had not awarded compensation for the alleged loss caused to the vehicle.

To that extent, the evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2, https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on:
08/10/2025 04:17:25 pm )
Crl .A.(MD)Nos.232 and 307 of 2017 Motor Vehicle Inspector and the investigating officer are sufficient to confirm that in the occurrence the vehicle was damaged.
27. The injured as well as the eyewitnesses to the occurrence, P.W.1 and P.W.2, stated clearly as to how the accused punched the front windshield of the car and had broken it.
The motor vehicle inspector has stated that the front windshield was about to crumble and it was shattered.
Such a condition of the car clearly constitutes damage.
The valuation of the damage might differ depending on the motor vehicle inspector's assessment and evaluation of the loss by the authority concerned.
Mere failure to get the loss certificate alone will not defeat case of the prosecution against the accused for the offence under Section 3(1) of TNPPDL Act, when the damage is very much patent.

Hence, in my considered view, the judgment of the trial Court with regard to the finding of the guilt against the accused for the offence under Section 3(1) of TNPPDL Act does not require any inference.

28. It is submitted by the learned counsel for the appellants that the accused persons are very young and hence, they may be shown some indulgence by being released on probation under the provisions of the probation of offender Act.
It might be true that the accused are first https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis
( Uploaded on: 08/10/2025 04:17:25 pm ) Crl.A.(MD)Nos.232 and 307 of 2017 offenders against whom no previous case is pending.
They did not realise their mistake and had chosen to admit their guilt at the very first instance by requesting the Court to invoke the provisions of Probation of Offenders' Act.
After causing mental agony to the victims to face trial and after getting the judgment of conviction and also filing the appeal by claiming innocent, now the request for probation is made.
The request for the said benefit have been made as last resort to escape from commission and not quite of genuine remorse or a desire to reform.

29. Though, in normal circumstances, the benefit of Probation of Offenders Act can be extended to the first offenders, the discretion is still vested with the Court to extend the same depending upon each case situation.
In the instant case, the accused do not deserve to be granted with the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
They are required to be punished for their audacious acts, which caused physical and mental agony to the victims and resulted in damage to their property.
30. However, considering the request of the learned counsel for the appellants and age of the accused, I feel to modify the sentence alone.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Only if the evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.2 are found to be unreliable in view of any significant reasons, the Court is required to seek the corroborative evidence that might be available through some independent witnesses.
Since P.W.1 and P.W.2 are the injured witnesses and victims, there exists no plausible motive for them to wrongly identify the accused.
As it pertains only to incidental facts that arose subsequent to the occurrence, the above contradiction can be ignored as a minor contradiction.
While appreciating the evidence in a holistic manner, the minor contradictions need to be overlooked.
19. Unless the evidence of injured witnesses, P.W. 1 and P.W.2, is tainted by any motive, there is no reason to doubt their evidence.
The occurrence took place on a public road, where P.W.1, the driver of the car, was driving the car by having P.W.2 also in the car.
Such indecent and barbaric conduct exhibited by the accused in the public view would have no doubt caused shame, embarrassment and pain to a woman like P.W.2.
In the above case, the Motor Vehicle Inspector advised the investigating officer to collect loss certificate, but in the instant case he did not give any direction.
Now, it is not a question of assessing the damage caused to the vehicle in order to grant any compensation.
The trial Court had imposed only fine and had not awarded compensation for the alleged loss caused to the vehicle.
The valuation of the damage might differ depending on the motor vehicle inspector's assessment and evaluation of the loss by the authority concerned.
Mere failure to get the loss certificate alone will not defeat case of the prosecution against the accused for the offence under Section 3(1) of TNPPDL Act, when the damage is very much patent.
They did not realise their mistake and had chosen to admit their guilt at the very first instance by requesting the Court to invoke the provisions of Probation of Offenders' Act.
After causing mental agony to the victims to face trial and after getting the judgment of conviction and also filing the appeal by claiming innocent, now the request for probation is made.
The request for the said benefit have been made as last resort to escape from commission and not quite of genuine remorse or a desire to reform.
29. Though, in normal circumstances, the benefit of Probation of Offenders Act can be extended to the first offenders, the discretion is still vested with the Court to extend the same depending upon each case situation.
In the instant case, the accused do not deserve to be granted with the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act.
opennyai_summary.decision:
They are required to be punished for their audacious acts, which caused physical and mental agony to the victims and resulted in damage to their property.
30. However, considering the request of the learned counsel for the appellants and age of the accused, I feel to modify the sentence alone.
In fine,
(i) These Criminal Appeals stand partly allowed by modifying the punishment by imposing a punishment of three months rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs.10,000/- in default to undergo one week simple imprisonment for the offense under Section 4 of TNPHW Act and by imposing three months rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs.10,000/-, in default to undergo one week rigorous imprisonment for the offence under Section 3 of TNPPDL Act.
The appeal remains confirmed and unaltered in all other aspects of the judgment of the Trial Court.
ii) The period of detention already undergone by the accused, if any, shall be given set off under Section 428 Cr.P.C and the sentences shall run concurrently.
(iii) The trial court shall take steps to secure the accused to commit him to prison to serve out the period of sentence.
